videos.script: Three web servers behind one load balancer look redundant. Lose a web server and the balancer routes around it. Lose the balancer and everything is gone. {{one}} So the balancer gets a twin. Two machines, and a choice about how they share the work. {{two}} In the first shape, one balancer does everything and the other waits. That is active-passive. In the second, both work, each on its own address. That is active-active. {{shapes}} In this lesson you build both in the lab's data centre, with HAProxy doing the balancing and keepalived moving the addresses. {{build}} You kill the active balancer in the middle of a stream of requests, and read the timestamps to see how long the site was gone. {{kill}} You stop a web server and watch the balancer take it out of rotation, then put it back. {{health}} And you see the rule that makes active-active honest. Each machine has to be able to carry everything alone, because one day it will. {{rule}} Last, the hard part a balancer cannot fix: the state a user's session leaves behind on one machine. {{state}}
